title: Cricket Scorecard System
description: Design a cricket scorecard tracker that manages innings, overs, balls, batsman strike rotation, wicket tracking, and extras. A **rules-heavy state machine** — the state hierarchy (match → innings → over → ball) is deep and each state transition has specific cricket rules governing it. Common in Indian company LLD interviews.
prompt: Design a cricket scorecard system that tracks live match data: innings, overs, runs, wickets, batsman stats, bowler stats, and extras.
prompt_note: Cricket has the most complex rule set of any LLD problem. The **state hierarchy** is nested 4 levels deep: Match → Innings → Over → Ball. Each ball delivery triggers: update batsman score, update bowler figures, track extras (wide/no-ball don't count as legal balls), rotate strike (on odd runs or end of over), check for innings end (all out / overs done / target reached). The interviewer is testing whether you can decompose these rules into clean entities without creating a God class.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Format — T20, ODI, or Test? That determines overs limit and innings count."
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Support configurable format. Start with T20 (20 overs, 2 innings). The design should work for ODI (50 overs) without changes."
clarifying_questions.why: Parameterize format — don't hardcode 20 overs. The state machine is the same regardless.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "What's a delivery? What inputs do we receive per ball?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Per ball: runs scored, extra type (WIDE, NO_BALL, BYE, LEG_BYE, NONE), wicket (type + dismissed batsman), and whether it was a boundary (4 or 6)."
clarifying_questions.why: Each delivery is a rich event with multiple outcomes happening simultaneously.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Strike rotation rules?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Odd runs → swap striker/non-striker. End of over → swap. Wide/no-ball → no strike change unless runs scored off them."
clarifying_questions.why: Strike rotation is the most common bug source. Model it explicitly.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Extras — do they count toward the bowler's figures?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Wide and no-ball: bowler concedes the runs + extras don't count as legal deliveries (over doesn't progress). Bye and leg-bye: legal delivery, runs go to extras not batsman, over progresses."
clarifying_questions.why: Each extra type has different scoring and legality rules.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Do we need full batsman and bowler stats?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Yes. Batsman: runs, balls faced, 4s, 6s, strike rate. Bowler: overs bowled, runs conceded, wickets, economy rate, maidens."
clarifying_questions.why: Two stat aggregation entities maintained in real time.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Winning condition?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Second innings: if batting team exceeds the target, they win. If all out or overs finish below target, bowling team wins. Draw/tie if scores are equal."
clarifying_questions.why: Simple comparison, but needs to be checked after every ball in the second innings.

core: **Match setup:** two teams, toss result (who bats first), overs limit, players per side (11).
**Ball-by-ball entry:** `recordBall(runs, extraType, wicket?, boundary?)` — the primary input.
**Over management:** 6 legal deliveries per over. Wide and no-ball don't count as legal. Auto-end over after 6 legal balls.
**Strike rotation:** swap on odd runs, swap at end of over. No swap on wide (unless runs scored).
**Wicket handling:** decrement available batsmen, update dismissed batsman stats, bring in next batsman.
**Innings end:** all out (10 wickets), overs exhausted, or target chased (2nd innings).
**Real-time stats:** batsman scorecard (runs, balls, 4s, 6s, SR), bowler scorecard (overs, maidens, runs, wickets, ER), team total, required run rate (2nd innings).
**Match result:** team 1 wins by X runs / team 2 wins by Y wickets / tie.
out_of_scope: Field placement, DRS (review system), DLS method (rain), player substitution, powerplay rules, free hit after no-ball, detailed wagon wheel, partnership tracking.

core: **Correctness above all:** cricket fans will notice any rule error. Over counting, extra rules, and strike rotation must be exact.
**Ball-by-ball granularity:** every delivery is recorded. Stats are incrementally updated, not batch-computed.
**Undo support (optional):** ability to correct the last ball entry if entered incorrectly.
out_of_scope: Persistence, real-time broadcasting, UI rendering, concurrent access (single scorer inputs data).

primary_scope: `recordBall(runs, extra, wicket?, boundary?)` → validate → update batsman → update bowler → update team score → handle extras → rotate strike → check over end → check innings end → check match end
Strike rotation: `(runs % 2 == 1) XOR (end of over)` → swap striker/non-striker
Innings end conditions: wickets == 10 || legalBalls == oversLimit * 6 || target chased
Stats computed incrementally on each ball
termination_points: `NoBatsmanAvailableException` — wicket falls but no batsman left to come in (innings should end)
entity_intro: The entity hierarchy mirrors the cricket structure: **Match** contains **Innings** (2 per match). Each Innings contains **Overs** (up to 20/50). Each Over contains **Balls** (up to 6 legal + extras). **Batsman** and **Bowler** scorecards aggregate across balls.

entities.name: Match
entities.role: **Controller.** Top-level. Holds both teams, innings list, match state (IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED), result. Delegates `recordBall` to the current innings.

entities.name: Team
entities.role: **Model.** teamName, `List<Player>` (11 players). Players have names and optional specialization (batsman/bowler/allrounder).

entities.name: Innings
entities.role: **Service.** Owns the current over, batting order (striker + non-striker + waiting list), bowler assignment, team total, wickets fallen, extras. Handles strike rotation and innings end detection.

entities.name: Over
entities.role: **Model.** overNumber, bowler reference, `List<Ball>`, legalBallCount. Ends when legalBallCount reaches 6. Tracks maiden (0 runs off the bat for the entire over).

entities.name: Ball
entities.role: **Model (immutable).** The atomic event: runs, extraType, wicket info, boundary flag, bowler, striker. One Ball per delivery.

entities.name: BatsmanScorecard
entities.role: **Model.** Per-batsman stats: runs, ballsFaced, fours, sixes, dismissalType. Updated on every ball faced.

entities.name: BowlerScorecard
entities.role: **Model.** Per-bowler stats: oversBowled (as decimal, e.g., 3.4), runsConceded, wickets, maidens. Updated on every ball bowled.

relationships.owns: battingTeam, bowlingTeam, `List<Over>`, currentOver, striker, nonStriker, `List<BatsmanScorecard>`, `Map<bowlerId, BowlerScorecard>`, totalRuns, totalWickets, totalExtras
runs, extraType, wicket, boundary, batsmanId, bowlerId

mvc_note: **MVC Mapping:** **Model** = Team, Player, Ball, BatsmanScorecard, BowlerScorecard, Over, ExtraType/WicketType/MatchState enums. **Service** = Innings (the complex state manager with strike rotation, over management, end detection). **Controller** = Match (public API: `recordBall`, `getScorecard`, `getResult`). The Innings class does the heavy lifting.
schema_note: **The `balls` table is the source of truth** — all stats can be recomputed from it. Scorecards (batsman/bowler) are materialized views updated incrementally. `(innings_id, over_number, ball_number)` gives exact ball-by-ball playback.

code_sections.label: Model — Enums + Ball + Scorecards
Service — Innings (the rules engine)
code_sections.flow: **`recordBall()` is the central method.** Steps: (1) create Ball object. (2) If WIDE/NO_BALL: add to extras, update bowler, but **don't count as legal ball** and **don't progress the over**. (3) If legal: increment batsman.facedBall(), add batsman runs, update bowler, increment over's legal count. (4) For BYE/LEG_BYE: legal delivery, runs go to extras not batsman. (5) If wicket: dismiss batsman, bring in next, check all-out. (6) Strike rotation: odd runs → swap. (7) Check over complete: if 6 legal balls → end over → swap strike → check maiden → start new over. (8) Check innings end: all out? Overs done? Target chased?
code_sections.edge_cases: Wide + wicket (stumping off a wide) → extra counted, wicket counted, not legal. No-ball + runs → batsman gets the runs, extra runs added too. Last wicket falls → innings ends (no need to bring in a new batsman). 2nd innings target chased mid-over → innings ends immediately. Bowler can't bowl consecutive overs.

code_sections.label: Controller — Match (top-level orchestration)

patterns.name: Hierarchical State Machine → Match > Innings > Over > Ball
patterns.why: The state hierarchy mirrors the real cricket structure: a match contains innings, an innings contains overs, an over contains balls. Each level has its own completion rules. Ball completion is trivial (one event). Over completes after 6 legal balls. Innings completes after all out / overs done / target chased. Match completes after both innings. This **nested FSM** is the natural model — don't flatten it.
patterns.where: `Match.recordBall()` → `Innings.recordBall()` → updates `Over` → checks completion at each level

patterns.name: Observer Pattern (extension) → Live Score Updates
patterns.why: Every ball is an event that could trigger UI updates, push notifications, commentary, and stat refreshes. In production, `recordBall` would fire an event that multiple listeners consume. Our simplified version computes everything synchronously.

patterns.name: Rules as Data
patterns.why: The extra-type scoring rules (WIDE = 1 penalty + not legal; BYE = legal + runs to extras) are implemented in a switch statement. For more complex rulesets (Test cricket, DLS), extract a `CricketRules` strategy that computes per-ball impacts. The Innings would call `rules.compute(ball)` and apply the returned state delta.
patterns.where: Currently inline in `Innings.recordBall()` switch — could be extracted

concurrency.issue: Not applicable in the core design
concurrency.fix: Cricket scoring is inherently single-threaded — one official scorer enters data ball by ball. No concurrent mutations. For a **live broadcast system** with thousands of readers, the scorecard would be published via an **event stream** (Kafka topic or WebSocket) — readers consume a projection, don't read from the mutable Innings directly.

deep_dives.question: How do you handle the complexity of extras and their different scoring rules?
deep_dives.answer: **Centralize in one place.** The switch statement in `recordBall()` handles all four extra types. Each type has exactly three properties: (1) is it a legal delivery? (2) who gets the runs (batsman or extras)? (3) does the bowler get charged? Encode this as a table: `WIDE={legal:false, batsmanRuns:false, bowlerCharged:true}`, `BYE={legal:true, batsmanRuns:false, bowlerCharged:false}`. The code reads the table and applies. If you add more extras (penalty runs, etc.), just add a row.

deep_dives.question: Why is strike rotation tricky?
deep_dives.answer: **Odd runs swap striker.** But: (1) Wide with no runs → no swap. (2) Wide + 1 run → swap (batsman ran). (3) End of over → swap (on top of any mid-over swaps). (4) Wicket might affect who's on strike (run-out of non-striker mid-run). Rule: swap happens independently for 'runs off bat' and 'end of over'. In code: `if (runs % 2 == 1) swap(); if (overComplete) swap();` — these compose correctly because XOR. **But on a wicket that's also the last ball of an over, the new batsman takes strike at the non-striker end.** Edge case city.

deep_dives.question: How would you implement undo (correct last ball)?
deep_dives.answer: **Memento Pattern.** Before each `recordBall`, snapshot the entire Innings state (totalRuns, totalWickets, striker/nonStriker references, bowler figures, over state). Store in a stack. On undo: pop the snapshot, restore state. **Alternative:** since balls are immutable events, maintain the ball list as the source of truth, and recompute the entire innings from scratch by replaying all balls. Slower but always correct. For T20 (max 240 balls), replay takes microseconds.

deep_dives.question: How would you support Test cricket (5-day, unlimited overs)?
deep_dives.answer: **Remove the `oversLimit` constraint.** Test innings end only on: all out, declaration (batting captain voluntarily ends), or follow-on. Add: `declare()` method on Innings. Match has 4 innings (not 2). Result: win by innings, win by runs, draw (not all innings completed in 5 days). The **state machine structure is identical** — just the completion conditions change. This is why parameterizing the format at construction time was important.

deep_dives.question: How would you add DLS (Duckworth-Lewis-Stern) for rain-affected matches?
deep_dives.answer: **Separate calculator service.** DLS takes: overs remaining, wickets lost, and uses published resource tables to compute a revised target. Add a `DLSCalculator` service injected into Match. When rain interrupts: `match.rainDelay(oversLost)` → `DLSCalculator.revisedTarget(oversRemaining, wicketsLost, firstInningsTotal)` → update `Innings.target`. **Don't embed DLS in the Innings class** — it's a separate algorithm that reads innings state. Classic Single Responsibility.

deep_dives.question: How would you generate a ball-by-ball commentary from this data?
deep_dives.answer: **Observer + Template.** Register a `CommentaryListener` on the match. On each ball event, the listener receives the Ball object + match context (score, overs, batsman). A `CommentaryTemplate` maps ball types to text: `{4 runs, boundary} → 'FOUR! Driven through covers!'`, `{wicket, bowled} → 'BOWLED! The stumps are shattered!'`. Templates can be randomized for variety. The match fires events; the commentary system consumes them. **Fully decoupled.** This is how ESPNcricinfo and Cricbuzz work internally.
